relations.note: Aganju is Ajaka’s son and successor in the principal Oyo genealogy.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 154–155

relations.note: Ajaka descends dynastically from Oduduwa through Ọ̀rànmíyàn; the intervening generations vary.
relations.source: Johnson and later Yoruba royal genealogies

relations.note: Some Bahian traditions treat Dadá Ajaká as a quality or form of Xangô.
relations.source: Querino, Verger, and later Bahian fieldwork

relations.note: One Bahian variant identifies Dadá Ajaká as Xangô’s mother.
Ṣàngó replaces the deposed Ajaka; Ajaka returns after Ṣàngó’s death.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 148–154

relations.note: Ṣàngó is Ajaka’s younger brother, or half-brother in some later accounts.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 148–154

relations.note: Bahian traditions variously describe Dadá Ajaká as Xangô’s elder brother or sister.
relations.source: Querino and Verger traditions summarized by Castillo

relations.note: Isola’s epilogue invokes divine judgment to moralize Ẹfúnṣetán’s death.
Later harmonized genealogy makes him Moremi's father-in-law through her marriage to his son Ọ̀rànmíyàn.
Beier makes Moremi's sacrifice reconcile Odùduwà's polity with the spirits of displaced landowners.
Festival performances symbolically oppose Obatala groups to Oduduwa and Oranmiyan groups.
Other Yoruba traditions make Oranmiyan the direct son of Oduduwa.
Johnson’s mythological scheme makes Oranmiyan the child of Oduduwa and Olokun.
relations.source: Johnson, The History of the Yorubas

relations.note: Johnson makes Oranmiyan Oduduwa’s grandson through Okanbi.
relations.source: Johnson, The History of the Yorubas

relations.note: Oranmiyan receives iron objects, a cock, and earth from Oduduwa’s divided property.
Ogun is Oranmiyan’s co-father and the source of his martial nature.
Olojo ritual associates their martial and iron-linked identities without equating them.
Johnson names Olokun as Oranmiyan’s mother and Oduduwa’s wife.
relations.source: Johnson, The History of the Yorubas

relations.note: Some later retellings connect Orunmila’s divination with Oranmiyan’s foundation of Oyo.
